text: Lessons 3 and 4 hardened Hartwell's four servers. This lesson builds the other half of the ask -- one real Sentinel rule watching for exactly the pattern a phished credential would produce if an attacker tried to use it. Hartwell's staff accounts sign in through Microsoft Entra ID, so every attempt lands in Sentinel's SigninLogs table.

The most direct starting query groups failures by user and by a ten-minute bucket, keeping only buckets with more than five failures. It's a real, runnable query -- but on its own it fires on any user with five-plus failures, whether or not a success ever followed. It isn't sequence-aware yet.

Making it sequence-aware means joining the failure logic against the user's successful sign-ins. A let-defined Failures query tracks the last failure time per cluster; a Successes query holds every successful sign-in; an inner join lines up each flagged user's failures with their own successes; and the final where clause keeps only a success that landed after the last failure, within a reasonable window.

That finished query gets pasted into a Scheduled Analytics Rule. Run query every ten minutes, matching the query's own bucket size. Lookup data from the last twenty minutes -- deliberately longer than the run frequency, so an event still being ingested right at the boundary doesn't fall into a gap between two runs. Alert threshold: greater than zero results.

Entity mapping is what makes the alert useful afterward -- mapping UserPrincipalName to the Account entity and IPAddress to the IP address entity, so Sentinel can correlate this alert with anything else touching the same user or address.
With the rule written and configured, next lesson tests it against sample sign-in data before it ever goes live -- confirming it fires on the real pattern and stays quiet on normal activity.
